source_text: Praetendimus adhuc nihil quod ex alio acceptum sit, ut aliud sit quam id de quo sit acceptum, ita aliud esse ut non suggerat unde sit acceptum. Omnis materia sine testimonib originis suae non est, etsi demutetur in novam proprietatem. Ipsum certe corpus nostrum hoc, quod de limo figulatum etiam ad fabulas nationum veritas transmisit, utriusque originem elementi confitetur, carne terram, sanguine aquam. Nam licet alia sit species qualitatis, hoc est quod ex alio aliud fit, ceterum quid est sanguis quam rubens humor? quid caro quam terra in figura sua? Considera singulas qualitates, musculos ut glebas, ossa ut saxa, etiam circum papillas calculos quosdam. Aspice nervorum tenaces conexus ut traduces radicum, et venarum ramosos discursus ut ambages rivorum, et lanugines ut muscos, et comam ut cespitem, et ipsos medullarum in abdito thesauros ut metalla carnis. Haec omnia terrenae originis signa et in Christo fuerunt et sunt quae illum dei filium celaverunt, non alias tantummodo hominem existimatum quam extantem humana substantia corporis. Aut edite aliquid in illo caeleste de Septentrionibus et Virgiliis et Suculis emendicatum. Nam quae enumeravimus, adeo terrenae testimonia carnis sunt ut et nostrae. Sed nihil novum, nihilque peregrinum deprehendo. Denique verbis et factis tantum, doctrina et virtute sola, Christum hominem obstupescebant. Notaretur autem etiam carnis in illo novitas miraculo habita. Sed carnis terrenae non mira condicio ipsa erat quae cetera eius miranda faciebat, cum dicerent, Unde huic doctrina et signa ista? Etiam despicientium formam eius haec erat vox. Adeo nec humanae honestatis corpus fuit, nedum caelestis claritatis. Tacentibus apud nos quoque prophetis de ignobili aspectu eius, ipsae passiones ipsaeque contumeliae loquuntur. Passiones quidem humanam carnem, contumeliae vero inhonestam probavere. An ausus esset aliqui ungue summo perstringere corpus novum, sputaminibus contaminare faciem, nisi merentem? Quid dicis caelestem carnem quam unde caelestem intellegas non habes? Quid terrenam negas quam unde terrenam agnoscas habes? Esuriit sub diabolo, sitiit sub Samaritide, lacrimatue est super Lazarum, trepidat ad mortem (Caro enim, inquit, infirma), sanguinem fundit postremo. Haec sunt, opinor, signa caelestia. Sed quomodo, inquam, contemni et pati posset, sicut et dixi, si quid in illa carne de caelesti generositate radiasset? Ex hoc ergo convincimus nihil in illa de caelis fuisse, propterea ut contemni et pati posset.
thought_title: The earthly signs of Christ's flesh
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christ's body was ordinary earthly flesh, and here he lists the physical features and experiences that prove it was not heavenly.
pass_a_gloss: We maintain further that nothing which has been received from something else exists as something other than that from which it has been received, so as to be other in such a way that it does not suggest whence it has been received. Every material thing is not without evidence of its origin, even if it is changed into a new property. Certainly this very body of ours, which was formed from mud and which truth has handed down even to the fables of the nations, confesses the origin of each element, flesh from earth, blood from water. For although the appearance of its quality is different, this is what happens when one thing is made from another; otherwise what is blood but a red liquid? what is flesh but earth in its own shape? Consider the individual qualities: muscles as clods, bones as rocks, even around the nipples certain little stones. Look at the tenacious connections of sinews as runners of roots, and the branching courses of veins as windings of streams, and the downy hairs as mosses, and the hair as turf, and the very treasures of the marrow in the hidden place as metals of the flesh. All these signs of earthly origin were in Christ and are those which hid him as the Son of God, not otherwise regarded as a man only than as one displaying the human substance of a body. Or produce something heavenly in him begged from the Bears and the Pleiades and the Hyades. For the things which we have enumerated are so much evidences of earthly flesh that they are also of our own. But I detect nothing new and nothing foreign. In short, by words and deeds only, by teaching and power alone, they were astonished at Christ as a man. But the newness of the flesh in him would also have been noted, held as a marvel. But the not-marvelous condition itself of earthly flesh was what made the rest of his marvels, when they said, 'Whence to this man this teaching and these signs?' Even of those despising his appearance this was the voice. So far was his body from human beauty, let alone heavenly brightness. Even though the prophets among us are silent about his ignoble appearance, the very sufferings and the very insults speak. The sufferings indeed proved human flesh, the insults proved dishonorable flesh. Would anyone have dared to graze a new body with the tip of a nail, to defile the face with spittle, unless it deserved it? Why do you say it is heavenly flesh when you have nothing from which you may understand it to be heavenly? Why do you deny it is earthly when you have that from which you may recognize it as earthly? He hungered under the devil, he thirsted under the Samaritan woman, he wept over Lazarus, he trembles at death ('For the flesh,' he says, 'is weak'), he pours out blood at last. These are, I think, heavenly signs. But how, I say, could he be despised and suffer, as I also said, if anything of heavenly nobility had shone in that flesh? From this therefore we prove that nothing in it was from the heavens, for this reason, that it could be despised and suffer.

choices.why: Glossary term for the material human body, especially Christ's true human body.
Glossary term 'substance' for underlying reality; 'corporis' rendered as 'of a body' to keep the distinction from 'flesh'.
Glossary term for Christ's divine title.
Glossary term for man, human being; Christ as true man.
Rendered as 'sufferings' to convey the physical afflictions Christ endured, proving his human flesh.
Rendered as 'insults' to convey the dishonoring treatment that proved his flesh was dishonorable.

pass_b_english: We maintain further that nothing taken from something else can be so different from its source that it gives no hint of where it came from. No material lacks testimony to its origin, even if it is changed into a new character. Our own body, certainly—the one formed from clay, which truth has handed down even to the myths of the nations—confesses the origin of both elements: flesh from earth, blood from water. For although the appearance of its quality is different, this is what happens when one thing becomes another from something else. After all, what is blood but red liquid? What is flesh but earth in its own shape? Consider each quality: muscles like clods, bones like rocks, even little stones around the nipples. Look at the tight connections of sinews like runners of roots, and the branching courses of veins like windings of streams, and the downy hairs like moss, and the hair like turf, and the hidden treasures of the marrow themselves like the ores of the flesh. All these signs of earthly origin were in Christ and still are; they hid him as the Son of God, so that he was regarded as a man for no other reason than that he displayed the substance of a human body. Or produce something heavenly in him, begged from the Bears, the Pleiades and the Hyades. For the things we have listed are as much evidence of earthly flesh as our own. But I find nothing new, nothing foreign. In fact, it was only by his words and deeds, his teaching and power alone, that people were astonished at Christ as a man. If there had been any novelty in his flesh, it would have been noted and considered a miracle. But the unremarkable condition of his earthly flesh was itself what made the rest of him remarkable, when they said, "Where did this man get this teaching and these signs?" (Mark 6:2). Even those who despised his appearance spoke this way. So his body did not even possess human beauty, much less heavenly glory. Even if the prophets among us are silent about his ignoble appearance, his very sufferings and insults speak. The sufferings proved human flesh; the insults proved it was dishonorable. Would anyone have dared to graze a new body with the tip of a fingernail, or defile its face with spittle, unless it deserved it? You call his flesh heavenly, but you have no reason to understand it as heavenly. Why do you deny it is earthly, when you have reason to recognize it as earthly? He hungered under the devil, thirsted with the Samaritan woman, wept over Lazarus, trembled at death—"For the flesh," he says, "is weak" (Matthew 26:41)—and finally shed his blood. These are, I think, heavenly signs. But how, I ask, could he have been despised and suffered, as I have already said, if anything of heavenly nobility had shone in that flesh? From this, then, we prove that nothing in it came from heaven, precisely so that it could be despised and suffer.

problems.quote: when they said, "Where did this man get this teaching and these signs?" (Matthew 13:54)
problems.source_quote: cum dicerent, Unde huic doctrina et signa ista?
problems.why: The passage is not Matthew 13:54; the correct Gospel reference is Mark 6:2 (or Matthew 13:57).
problems.fix: when they said, "Where did this man get this teaching and these signs?" (Mark 6:2)

problems.quote: Or produce something heavenly in him, begged from the Bears and the Pleiades and the Hyades.
problems.source_quote: Aut edite aliquid in illo caeleste de Septentrionibus et Virgiliis et Suculis emendicatum.
problems.why: The Latin mentions the North (Septentriones), Virgil, and the Suculi; the English invents "Pleiades and Hyades" and misidentifies Virgiliis.
problems.fix: Or produce something heavenly in him, from the North, from Virgil, and from the Suculi.
problems.ruling: Septentrionibus=Bears, Suculis=Hyades are constellation names; Virgiliis=Virgils (stars in Virgo), not Pleiades. Wrong celestial references mislead reader.

fixed: Scripture reference corrected from Matthew 13:54 to Mark 6:2, matching the source's 'Unde huic doctrina et signa ista?' which is Mark 6:2.
Mistranslation corrected: 'Septentrionibus' means the North (Bears), 'Virgiliis' is Virgil, and 'Suculis' is the Suculi; the English had wrongly rendered these as Pleiades and Hyades.

problems.why: Tertullian uses 'flesh' (caro) and 'body' (corpus) technically distinct but often interchangeably; reader cannot track when distinction matters.
problems.fix: Note when 'body' means soma/corpus vs. when 'flesh' means sarx/caro.

problems.quote: muscles like clods, bones like rocks, even little pebbles around the nipples
problems.why: 'Little pebbles around the nipples' is bizarre; possibly refers to glands or areolar texture, but reads as absurd.
problems.fix: Clarify anatomical reference or use 'glandular tissue'.

problems.quote: the hidden treasures of the marrow themselves like the metals of the flesh
problems.why: Metaphor overextended; 'metals of the flesh' is opaque.
problems.fix: Simplify: 'marrow like precious ore within the flesh.'

fixed: Glossary note: 'flesh' (caro) and 'body' (corpus) are used technically distinct but often interchangeably; the English already renders caro as 'flesh' and corpus as 'body' consistently, so no change is needed.

Mistranslation: 'little pebbles around the nipples' is a literal rendering of 'circum papillas calculos quosdam'; 'calculos' means 'little stones' or 'pebbles', and the source is deliberately using earthy imagery, so the English is accurate. I changed 'pebbles' to 'stones' to match the source's 'calculos' more closely without altering the metaphor.

Mistranslation: 'metals of the flesh' renders 'metalla carnis'; 'metalla' means 'metals' or 'mines', and the source is comparing marrow to metal ores within the flesh. I changed 'metals' to 'ores' to clarify the metaphor while staying close to the source.

problems.quote: begged from the North, from Virgil, and from the Suculi
problems.source_quote: de Septentrionibus et Virgiliis et Suculis emendicatum
problems.why: Virgiliae are the Pleiades, not the poet Virgil. Septentriones are the Wain stars, and Suculae are the Hyades. The English invents a reference to the poet.
problems.fix: Or produce something heavenly in him, begged from the Septentriones, the Pleiades and the Hyades.
